summary: L&T builds buildings, transport links and energy facilities, makes specialised equipment, and has businesses providing computer and engineering services, loans and property development.
description: Imagine an organisation needing a bridge, factory or energy facility. It can hire L&T to design and build specified work rather than do every task itself. The wider group also provides services such as software and lending, which have different customers and costs from construction.
money: Project customers pay for agreed design, equipment supply and construction. Other customers pay for manufactured equipment or technology work; borrowers pay interest and charges on loans. The group must cover materials, workers, suppliers, funding and other costs before these activities produce profit.
customers: Government bodies and infrastructure owners, energy and industrial companies, technology clients, property buyers and borrowers. Each pays for a defined asset, piece of equipment, service or access to money.
drivers: Winning workable contracts, carrying out the work at the agreed cost, getting customer approval, collecting payment and funding staff, equipment and other commitments while work continues.

groups.title: Building infrastructure
groups.examples: Buildings, factories, transport links, water works and power-network projects.
groups.explanation: The customer buys specified construction work or a completed asset. Designs, permits, materials, suppliers and site workers have to be organised. A bridge contract is a job to perform over time, not cash earned at the moment it is announced.

groups.title: Building energy facilities
groups.examples: Engineering and construction for oil, gas, power and related energy projects.
groups.explanation: An energy company can buy L&T’s work to build or equip a facility. L&T does not have to own the facility or sell the energy itself. Technical requirements, the customer’s decisions and site readiness affect delivery.

groups.title: Making specialised equipment
groups.examples: Heavy engineering, precision systems and industrial equipment.
groups.explanation: Customers buy equipment made for demanding applications. Engineers, suitable materials, factory work and testing are needed before the buyer accepts it; selling more units is not the only measure of useful work.

groups.title: Technology and engineering services
groups.explanation: A client pays skilled people to develop, maintain or improve systems or designs. Staffing, the work agreed and the client’s technology budget matter more than a construction site’s progress.

groups.title: Loans through L&T Finance
groups.explanation: The customer borrows money and pays interest, the charge for using it, under the loan terms. The lender must obtain funds, assess whether borrowers can repay and collect the money. A growing loan book, meaning loans outstanding, does not guarantee that all borrowers will pay.

groups.title: Property and other development businesses
groups.examples: Property development, relevant infrastructure investments and industrial products.
groups.explanation: Developing property or owning an infrastructure investment can require spending before sales or operating income arrives. This differs from a customer paying L&T to build for them. Check who owns the project and which company receives the payments.

basics.title: What does engineering, procurement and construction mean?
basics.text: This kind of contract (EPC) covers designing the project, buying the materials and equipment, and building it. The contract says which tasks the company must complete, what the customer pays and who bears delays or extra costs.

basics.title: An order is work still to be done
basics.text: The order book is the value of accepted work waiting to be carried out. Some jobs take a long time, change or are cancelled. A signed order is therefore different from work already earned, billed or paid for.

steps.title: Understand the job and agree terms
steps.text: Estimate the work, suppliers, timetable, risks and price before accepting the order.

steps.title: Design, buy and build
steps.text: Arrange engineers, materials, equipment and workers, then manage the agreed factory or site work.

steps.title: Record progress and obtain approval to bill
steps.text: The accounts can record earned work before every billing condition has been met. Customers may need to inspect or certify completed stages.

steps.title: Collect payment and finish the remaining duties
steps.text: Receive amounts due, hand over work and meet testing, repair or warranty promises. Some customer payment may be held back until later conditions are satisfied.

specifics.title: A fixed price can leave the contractor with extra costs
specifics.text: If the agreed price stays fixed while labour or materials become dearer, L&T may bear the increase. Other contracts allow certain costs to be passed to the customer. Order size alone does not explain this risk.

specifics.title: Progress, a bill and cash are separate stages
specifics.text: Work recorded before it can be billed without further conditions is called a contract asset. A receivable is an amount due from a customer. Retention is payment held back until specified conditions are met. None means all the money has already arrived.

specifics.title: Lending and software need their own questions
specifics.text: A construction job depends on completing the project. A software service depends on client demand and skilled staff. A lender must collect repayments and cover the cost of obtaining its funds. The same performance measure cannot explain all three equally well.

watch: Can signed orders actually move into work?
Customers still need funding, approvals and ready sites.
Read the type of contract, timetable, country and customer readiness. Keep possible bids separate from signed orders and ask what could delay the work the company has already accepted.
Does the agreed payment cover the cost of doing the job?
Long projects can face changing material, labour and supplier costs.

Check whether the price is fixed or can change with costs. Read delays, claims for extra work and the business’s reported result together instead of assuming a large new order carries the same profit as earlier work.
Are completed stages turning into cash?
Work can be recorded before the customer approves a bill or pays it.

Read contract assets, customer amounts due, retained payments and advances received. Compare them with cash generated by operations, and investigate older or disputed claims rather than counting them as collected money.
Are technology clients and borrowers paying as expected?
Service work and loans have different risks from building a project.
Read technology demand and staffing costs separately from lending growth, funding costs and missed repayments. Check which companies are included in the group figures before comparing their earnings.
Do investments eventually produce useful cash returns?
Property, infrastructure holdings and new facilities can require spending first.

Read money invested with the asset’s progress, income and cash received. Check debt and guarantees, which can require payment if agreed conditions occur, and separate normal activity from one-off gains on selling an asset.
risks: The annual report says trade tariffs, port congestion, closed airspace and changed shipping routes have made deliveries of imported materials slower and dearer, which can stretch project timelines.

West Asia is one of L&T’s main overseas markets. The annual report says the conflict there has raised security risks and insurance and shipping costs, and made new investment in the region less certain.
As the world shifts from oil and gas to renewable power, the annual report calls this a material risk for L&T’s oil-and-gas construction business, even as it creates solar, wind and storage work.
Clients are using AI tools to write and test software themselves. The annual report says L&T’s technology-services companies must change what they offer as a result.
Customers usually require bank guarantees while a project is built and sometimes after. L&T must keep enough bank credit lines to provide them.
context: The Hyderabad metro sale is agreed but not yet completed

L&T’s results for the quarter to 30 September 2026, published on 27 October 2026, say it agreed on 29 April 2026 to sell its whole stake in L&T Metro Rail (Hyderabad) Limited, the company that runs the Hyderabad metro, to a Telangana government company. The sale is still in progress, with expected completion moved to 31 December 2026. Until then the accounts show the metro business as “held for sale”: kept separate because it is expected to leave the group. An agreed sale and a completed, paid sale are different stages. The same results also rename L&T’s reporting groups from 1 April 2026. For example, Infrastructure Projects is now Infrastructure & Utilities, IT & Technology Services is now Technology, Platforms & Services, and solar and wind construction now sits in a new Energy – Green group. The audited 2025–26 figures below use the older names.
sources: FY 2025–26 integrated annual report (risk management framework, outlook)
Quarter and half-year results, metro sale status and renamed reporting segments · 27 October 2026

financialNotes.title: Read construction size separately from earnings leadership
financialNotes.text: The verified consolidated table groups several types of business. Infrastructure Projects has the largest revenue, while IT & Technology Services has the largest reported segment result in this period. That result is not net profit or cash collected.

financialNotes.title: Internal work and group adjustments still matter
financialNotes.text: Reported segment revenue includes internal sales, which are removed when reconciling to net group revenue. Other finance costs, unallocated items, exceptional items and tax also separate the segment-result total from company profit.

stepsTitle: From a contract to a finished project.

quick.title: What it does
quick.text: L&T builds buildings, transport links and energy plants, makes specialised equipment, and has businesses that provide computer and engineering services, loans and property.

quick.title: Who pays
quick.text: Government bodies, infrastructure owners, energy and industrial companies, technology clients, property buyers and borrowers. Each pays for a defined project, item, service or loan.

quick.title: How it earns
quick.text: Project customers pay as agreed design, supply and building work is done and approved. Other parts earn from equipment, technology services, loan interest and property sales.

quick.title: What it spends on
quick.text: Materials, workers, suppliers and subcontractors, equipment, and the cost of funding work while it is under way.

helps.title: Many businesses in many countries
helps.text: Construction, equipment, technology services, lending and property depend on different customers. The annual report says this mix and L&T’s presence in many countries help it cope when one area weakens.

helps.title: Years of work already won
helps.text: L&T’s order book, the work customers have agreed to but L&T has not yet done, was at a record high in March 2026, and about half of it was abroad. The annual report says this gives it several years of visible revenue.

helps.title: India keeps building
helps.text: The annual report expects India’s economy to keep growing on the back of household spending and steady government spending on infrastructure, the kind of project L&T builds.

hurts.title: Projects run late
hurts.text: Big sites face land-access problems, difficult ground, slow approvals, design changes and shortages of workers. Each can delay billing and add cost.

hurts.title: Metal and cement prices jump
hurts.text: Steel, cement, aluminium and copper are a large share of project costs. On fixed-price contracts, a price rise after bidding can come out of L&T’s margin.

hurts.title: Tough price competition
hurts.text: Government work is usually won through competitive bidding, and rivals in India and abroad may bid aggressively. That squeezes margins and can cost L&T projects.

hurts.title: Disagreements over contracts
hurts.text: Long projects with many parties, slow approvals or unclear contract terms can lead to disagreements with customers over who pays for what.
